Saudi Arabia Expands Oil Storage in Japan as Tokyo Restocks

Julianne Geiger is a veteran energy journalist and market analyst with more than a decade of experience covering the global oil and gas sector. Her…

Japan plans to buy up to 8 million barrels of Saudi crude for the national petroleum reserve it drew down during the Hormuz crisis, under a deal the two countries announced on Friday that makes the purchases subject to favorable market conditions. The deal also gives Saudi Arabia temporary use of an additional 16 million barrels of storage capacity in Japan, expanding the 8 million barrels it already holds there, and the kingdom has begun refilling those tanks, Bloomberg reported.

Under the existing arrangement with Saudi Aramco, Japan gets preferential rights to purchase the Saudi crude stored in its facilities during a supply emergency. Aramco can sell that oil to other Asian customers under normal conditions, but Japan gets first access when supplies are disrupted.

Middle Eastern crude made up more than 90% of Japan’s imports before the war. When Iranian attacks all but shut the Strait of Hormuz, Japan bought cargoes from as far away as Canada, Azerbaijan and Africa to keep its refiners running. Tokyo released oil from its national reserves last month as part of the International Energy Agency’s coordinated drawdown, in which member countries agreed to release a record 400 million barrels.

Gulf crude exports recovered to 82% of prewar levels in October, according to the IEA, and the question for the market now is when importers will start buying back what they released. Brent traded around $92 a barrel on Thursday, down from above $110 in October, and Goldman Sachs expects a sizable surplus next year that will push prices lower.

Producers are building their own buffers closer to their customers. Saudi Arabia has held talks with foreign governments to give Aramco access to their strategic storage, and Singapore announced plans last month to store Saudi crude in its Jurong Rock Caverns during the second half of 2027.

Tokyo wants a regional system on top of the bilateral deals. Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi this week proposed a joint Asian task force to manage crude stockpiles, which she described as an Asian version of the IEA. ASEAN members have separately agreed on a shared reserve with storage sites in Indonesia and Thailand, coordinated by the Philippines.
